messages.subject: INLA  coast Boundary mesh problem
parts:
Hi Everyone,
My name is Morgane. I am a PhD student from the University of Aberdeen. I am building an INLA Spatio-temporal log-Gaussian Cox Processes model to assess the distribution of birds in the Firth of Forth area.I am having problems building the INLA mesh. I am trying to build my mesh by point locations(long and lat) and point id numbers from the data_df.txt file.I am also using the FOF_bound_sf file which is the shapefile of the coastal boundary called Coast_FVCOM_bound_shapefile.shp for my mesh. I attached and plotted the data in the zip file. Plot_1, shows the red dots which are the locations of the points to create the mesh triangles inside the FOF_bound_sf. In Plot_2, I am creating the mesh using inla. mesh.create () function, but the mesh seems to be outside my FOF_bound_sf and not inside. In detail, I want my mesh triangles to be inside the blue boundary but at the moment the mesh seems to be created outside the blue boundary (Plot_2).I attached the R code, the data, plot_1 and plot _2 in the zip file.Would you have any advice to solve this problem?

Thank you in advance 
Morgane

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
parts:
Hi,

the INLA/fmesher code, as well as the "sf" standard, defines the
interior of a polygon by what direction the boundary is traversed,
specifically counterclockwise for the boundary of a polygon when seen
from "above".
Unfortunately, lots of code either has a different convention, or
fails to properly convert between the two different conventions (e.g.
the geos library has a clockwise convention, but the "sf" package
ignores that, so whenever sf calls
a libgeos method with a properly counterclockwise oriented polygon,
libgeos converts it to its clockwise convention, and sf doesn't
convert it back again afterwards).
There are different ways of "fixing" such polygons (but in general it
is impossible to "fix" as both orientations potentially carry
information that is lost when assuming the polygon should have a
certain orientation).
One is to reverse the coordinate order, and another is to ask sf to
guess the correct orientation, which is probably the easiest approach:

data$geometry <- sf::st_sfc(data$geometry, check_ring_dir = TRUE)

But apart from that, you might need to consider having an extension
outside the blue boundary as well; the edge in the ocean isn't a "hard
boundary", so having the model extend a bit would remove the spde
model boundary effects from the domain of interest. You can have
larger triangles in that outer extension, so the computational cost is
only increased slightly.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
parts:
See example code at
https://inlabru-org.github.io/fmesher/articles/basic_use.html
The principle is this:
fm_mesh_2d(..., boundary = list(first_boundary, outer_boundary),
max.edge = c(inner_max_edge, outer_max_edge))

Note that extending the mesh inland is also ok, for the same reason,
unless you need the structure to "block" the path between different
parts of the ocean. But in that case, you could apply a barrier spde
model to the mesh instead of the default spde models.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA coast Boundary mesh problem
parts:
Since the birds can fly over land, and there’s no reason to assume Neumann spde boundaries to be better at the coastline than a stationary model, you can simply ignore the estimation results over land. That they exist in the computational model doesn’t mean you need to interpret them in any way.

The barrier model would be needed e.g. if you were modelling fish in an archipelago, where they cannot swim across islands.

Finn
